issues.legal_issue: Heirs who normally resided with a tenant in a residential building at the time of the tenant’s death become tenants individually rather than as a single body of joint tenants.
material_facts: The deceased tenant’s widow, sons, and daughter normally lived with him in the residential premises when he died.
They continued to live in the premises after his death, and rent continued to be paid.
issues.conclusion: The heirs who satisfied the statutory residence requirement became tenants in their own right; they did not collectively become joint tenants.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 defines the tenant of a residential building after the tenant’s death to include only heirs who normally resided with the tenant in the building at the time of death. Each qualifying heir becomes a tenant in his or her own right. Section 3(g) defines the tenant’s family for purposes including Section 12(3). The Court rejected the joint-tenancy approach adopted in Smt. Rama Devi Shakya, 1981 Allahabad Rent Cases 305.

predicates.residential_rent_control_tenancy_proceed: The proceeding concerns a residential tenancy governed by rent-control regulation.
predicates.tenant_died: The tenant died while the residential tenancy existed.
predicates.heirs_normally_resided_with_tenant_at_de: The heirs in question normally lived with the tenant in the rented home when the tenant died.

issues.definition: When a residential rent-control tenancy continues after the tenant’s death, heirs who normally lived with the tenant in the home at death become tenants individually.

issues.legal_issue: A residential building acquired by one qualifying heir does not terminate the separate tenancies of other qualifying heirs who continue occupying the tenanted building.
material_facts: The deceased tenant’s heirs who normally lived with him in the premises continued to live there after his death and became tenants in their own right.
One son built another residential house in the same city and moved into it.
The other heirs continued to occupy the original premises, but the authorities treated that premises as vacant because of the son’s acquisition.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition and occupation of another house by one heir did not terminate the tenancies of the other heirs, and the original premises did not become vacant on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Section 12(3) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 deems a tenant to have ceased occupying a residential building when the tenant or a member of the tenant’s family builds or acquires another residential building in the same city. Read with the separate-tenancy definition in Section 3(a) and the family definition in Section 3(g), the provision applies to the relevant tenant and that tenant’s family; it does not extinguish the independent tenancies of other heirs. The Court rejected the contrary conclusion in Smt. Rama Devi Shakya, 1981 Allahabad Rent Cases 305, reasoning that the Act did not make all qualifying heirs joint tenants and that the contrary reading could impose severe hardship.

predicates.residential_rent_control_deemed_vacancy_: The proceeding concerns whether a residential building is deemed vacant under rent-control regulation.
predicates.multiple_heirs_are_individual_tenants: More than one heir qualified as a tenant of the residential home in his or her own right after the original tenant’s death.
predicates.one_heir_acquired_another_residence_in_t: One of those heirs built or acquired another residential home in the same city and occupied it.
predicates.other_heirs_continued_occupying_the_tena: The other qualifying heirs continued to live in the original rented home.

issues.definition: If one heir with an individual tenancy acquires another residence in the same city, the other individual tenants who remain in the rented home retain their tenancies and that home is not deemed vacant on that basis.
